lessons.title: Orientation & Safety

learningObjectives.statement: Set up a comfortable and accessible practice session before entering immersive learning.
Describe the app's hand-tracking, emergency-call and completion-record limits.
Choose a dominant hand and input method, then complete an unscored knowledge check.

contentBlocks.title: Training scope
contentBlocks.body: Lifesaver Vision is a practice academy. Where an activity offers practice feedback, it is limited to sequence, hand-placement zone, rhythm, interruptions and posture heuristics. Hand tracking does not measure physical compression depth or force; those fields remain labelled ‘Not physically assessed’ unless a verified external CPR sensor is connected.

contentBlocks.title: SIMULATION — 995
contentBlocks.body: Every 995 interaction in the academy is clearly labelled SIMULATION. It rehearses communication only and never places a telephone call.

contentBlocks.title: Leave immersion at any time
contentBlocks.body: Use the persistent Exit Simulation control whenever you feel uncomfortable or want to return to the shared-space dashboard. Learning progress is not treated as clinical performance merely because an immersive session was opened or closed.

contentBlocks.title: Comfort calibration
contentBlocks.body: Before practice, position the learning volume comfortably with the available system controls, confirm that the floor and nearby space are clear, and use a seated or standing presentation only where the activity allows it. These are learner comfort checks rather than stored calibration measurements. Stop the immersive session whenever comfort changes.

contentBlocks.title: Dominant hand and input
contentBlocks.body: Confirm your dominant hand and preferred supported input method in the device's accessibility and input settings before practice. This release does not store a separate in-app dominant-hand profile. Input choices do not change the clinical sequence being taught.

contentBlocks.title: Accessibility setup
contentBlocks.body: Use device text-accessibility settings as needed. In the app, set captions, audio level, increased contrast and reduced motion before starting. Knowledge checks are untimed and can be reopened for review without penalty.

contentBlocks.title: Hand-data handling
contentBlocks.body: Hand-tracking permission is optional. When a supported practice activity requests it, hand position and motion are processed on the device; the declared hand-tracking purpose states that this data is not stored. The current permission service alone does not provide CPR-quality measurements.

contentBlocks.title: Learning records and privacy
contentBlocks.body: The local-first LMS may retain progress, attempts, feedback, sign-off and learning-event records. Learners can export their local record and request local deletion through the privacy controls. The privacy manifest declares no tracking and no collected-data categories.

contentBlocks.title: Completion is not accreditation
contentBlocks.body: Course completion produces an internal completion record only. It is not SRFAC certification. Practical competency requires a qualified instructor's recorded sign-off.

contentBlocks.title: Request instructor assessment
contentBlocks.body: After completing the adult core and practice activities, ask a qualified instructor to schedule a practical assessment. The current learner interface does not submit that request automatically. An instructor may approve the practical sign-off or return focused remediation; self-completion cannot replace that decision.

contentBlocks.title: Pre-course knowledge check
contentBlocks.body: The six-question check establishes a starting point. It is unscored, untimed and does not block learning; every answer review links to a source-checked clinical fact.

The casualty is awake and reports ankle pain
The casualty is asleep and breathing normally
The casualty is conscious and coughing

questions.explanation: Cardiac arrest causes loss of consciousness and absence of normal breathing because the heart has stopped pumping blood effectively.

As a reason to delay assessment for one minute

Leave the casualty and make the call from another room

40 to 60 compressions per minute
70 to 80 compressions per minute

Hold both pads firmly against the chest
Continue moving the casualty
Disconnect the pads

learningObjectives.statement: Distinguish cardiac arrest from a heart attack using the supported warning and recognition facts.

sourceReferences.section: 1.5 What Happens in a Cardiac Arrest
1.4 What Happens in a Heart Attack

learningObjectives.statement: Explain why recognition, compressions and defibrillation are time-critical.
Recognise gasping as abnormal breathing and interpret the supplied 2019 Singapore OHCA figures.

contentBlocks.title: What cardiac arrest means
contentBlocks.body: During cardiac arrest the heart is no longer pumping blood. The casualty becomes unresponsive and does not breathe normally; ventricular fibrillation develops in many arrests.

sourceReferences.section: 1.5 What Happens in a Cardiac Arrest

contentBlocks.title: Heart attack and cardiac arrest are different
contentBlocks.body: A heart attack begins with a blocked coronary artery and can progress to cardiac arrest if untreated. Warning signs supported by the source include chest or upper-abdominal tightness or discomfort, possible spread towards the left shoulder or arm, neck or lower jaw, sudden breathlessness, sweating, nausea, vomiting or dizziness. The source directs calling 995 and going to an Emergency Department.

sourceReferences.section: 1.4 What Happens in a Heart Attack

contentBlocks.title: Minutes matter
contentBlocks.body: Brain cells begin to die within about four to six minutes after cardiac arrest, and irreversible injury may begin at roughly four minutes without restored circulation. The supplied manuals report survival near 90% with immediate reversal, around 40–50% at six minutes and about 10% by nine minutes.

contentBlocks.title: Shockable rhythms
contentBlocks.body: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are shockable rhythms. The supplied sources report that survival from VF falls by about 7–10% for each minute treatment is delayed; untreated VF can deteriorate to asystole, which is not shockable and is managed with CPR.

contentBlocks.title: Gasping is not normal breathing
contentBlocks.body: Agonal gasps do not count as normal breathing. If breathing is absent or abnormal, or you are unsure, begin chest compressions immediately.

contentBlocks.title: Singapore OHCA snapshot
contentBlocks.body: The 2019 registry recorded 3,233 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in Singapore. About 74% occurred at home; bystander CPR occurred in 60%, bystander defibrillation in 10.5%, overall survival was 6.2%, and 4.8% were discharged with good-to-moderate neurological function.

contentBlocks.title: Guideline update: use the 2019 registry
contentBlocks.body: The 2018 manual presented older 2015 registry figures. This course uses the later 2019 figures contained in the 2022 manual; the older values appear only as historical context.

contentBlocks.title: Anatomy scope
contentBlocks.body: This release does not add detailed heart or lung anatomy beyond the circulation, breathing and rhythm facts in the approved extract. Any spatial visual used with this lesson is an orientation aid, not a diagnostic or anatomical reference.

modules.title: Chain of Survival
modules.summary: The current seven-ring learning sequence, its meanings and the documented source disagreement.

lessons.title: Chain of Survival
lessons.summary: The current seven-ring learning sequence, its meanings and the documented source disagreement.

learningObjectives.statement: Describe the meaning of each current Chain of Survival ring while recognising that the preferred ring count and graphic await SME confirmation.
Explain why early CPR and early defibrillation work together.
Identify what changed from the five-ring 2018 presentation to the seven-ring 2022 presentation.

contentBlocks.title: Current learning sequence — seven rings
contentBlocks.body: The course's active, review-gated learning sequence provisionally follows the 2022 provider manual: Prevention; Early Activation and AED Access; Early CPR; Early Defibrillation; Emergency Medical Services (Ambulance); Advanced Cardiac Life Support; Recovery. The two current supplied sources differ on the graphic and ring count, so this card is excluded from scoring until a qualified SME approves the presentation.

contentBlocks.title: What the rings mean
contentBlocks.body: Prevention covers reducing risk through a healthy lifestyle and regular checks. Activation means calling 995, following the dispatcher and arranging a nearby visible AED through another person; a lone rescuer stays with the casualty. Early CPR means starting promptly because brain cells can begin dying within four to six minutes. Early Defibrillation means applying a community AED and being ready to shock. EMS and advanced hospital care continue treatment, and Recovery represents rehabilitation and community support.

sourceReferences.section: 2.2 (A) Ask someone to get an AED

contentBlocks.title: CPR and defibrillation belong together
contentBlocks.body: The supplied historic outcome chart shows the strongest survival when CPR, defibrillation and advanced care begin very early, compared with no CPR and a delayed shock.

contentBlocks.title: What changed since the 2018 manual?
contentBlocks.body: The 2018 manual taught five rings. The 2022 manual adds Prevention and Recovery to form seven, while the 2021 update deck still shows five. Lifesaver Vision follows the 2022 sequence for learning, labels the disagreement, and keeps ring-count questions out of scored assessment pending SME approval.

interactiveActivities.instructions: Explore each ring meaning. The seven-ring visual remains labelled clinical review required and contributes no score.

questions.prompt: What does the Prevention concept emphasise?

choices.text: Healthy living and regular health checks can reduce risk
Waiting for symptoms before considering health
Using an AED on every conscious person
Avoiding all physical activity

questions.explanation: Prevention concerns reducing risk through a healthy lifestyle and regular check-ups.

questions.prompt: Which action belongs to Early Activation and AED Access?

choices.text: Call 995, follow the dispatcher and arrange for an AED
Wait silently for someone else to notice
Delay calling until after the third AED analysis
Drive the casualty to hospital before calling

questions.explanation: Early activation means contacting 995, following the dispatcher and arranging prompt AED access.

questions.prompt: Why should Early CPR begin promptly?

choices.text: Brain cells can begin dying within four to six minutes
It guarantees that an AED will not be needed
It replaces the need to call 995
It is useful only after twenty minutes

questions.explanation: Early CPR should begin quickly because brain cells can begin dying within four to six minutes.

questions.prompt: What is the rescuer's role in Early Defibrillation?

choices.text: Apply a community AED and be ready to follow a shock prompt
Guess the heart rhythm without an AED
Deliver a shock before pads are attached
Turn off the AED as soon as it begins analysing

questions.explanation: Early Defibrillation means applying an AED promptly and being ready to follow its shock instructions.

questions.prompt: What support is associated with Recovery after survival?

choices.text: Community and medical rehabilitation support
Immediate removal of all medical follow-up
AED analysis without pads
Delaying transport for several hours

questions.explanation: Recovery includes community and medical rehabilitation support for a survivor.

questions.prompt: Which combination is associated with the best chance of survival?

choices.text: Early CPR together with early defibrillation
Delayed CPR without arranging an AED
Waiting for the casualty to recover without intervention
Defibrillation without first applying pads

questions.explanation: Survival is highest when early CPR is combined with early defibrillation.

learningObjectives.statement: Apply DRSABC in order and branch safely for unsafe scenes, responsiveness and breathing.

sourceReferences.section: RCA adult BLS algorithm for lay rescuers

learningObjectives.statement: Rehearse a clearly labelled simulated 995 call using speaker mode and dispatcher guidance.
Choose correct AED retrieval behaviour when a bystander is present or the rescuer is alone.

sourceReferences.section: 2.2 (A) Ask someone to get an AED

contentBlocks.title: DRSABC
contentBlocks.body: Move through DRSABC in order: first assess Danger, then test Responsiveness; Shout for help and activate 995; Ask another person for an AED; decide whether Breathing is normal; and begin continuous Chest Compressions when normal breathing is absent or uncertain. A pulse check appears only in the clearly labelled trained-healthcare-provider path.

contentBlocks.title: Danger comes first
contentBlocks.body: Confirm the area is safe before helping. Give care where the person is found unless traffic, flames, a slippery surface, falling objects or another hazard makes the location unsuitable. If so, promptly relocate the casualty to a clear, level place where care can continue safely.

contentBlocks.title: Responsiveness and position
contentBlocks.body: Tap the shoulders firmly and ask loudly whether the casualty is okay. Do not shake violently or move the neck unnecessarily. Effective CPR needs the casualty on their back on a firm, flat surface; if turning is required, support and turn the head, neck and body together.

contentBlocks.title: SIMULATION — 995 call rehearsal
contentBlocks.body: This rehearsal never dials. In the scenario, call 995, use speaker mode, stay on the line, answer the simulated dispatcher's questions and hang up only when told. Follow the simulated dispatcher's coaching.

contentBlocks.title: Dispatcher support
contentBlocks.body: The supplied sources state that a 995 dispatcher can locate a nearby AED, summon trained volunteers in the vicinity and coach chest compressions. Volunteer myResponder participation is voluntary.

contentBlocks.title: Bystander available or alone
contentBlocks.body: When another person is available, ask them to fetch an AED that is within about a 60-second walk. When you are the lone rescuer, stay with the casualty and begin compressions rather than leaving to search for an AED.

sourceReferences.section: 2.2 (A) Ask someone to get an AED

contentBlocks.title: Guideline update: the lone rescuer stays
contentBlocks.body: The 2018 manual allowed a lone rescuer to fetch an AED when it was visible and nearby. Current supplied guidance says the lone rescuer must not leave the casualty; another person should retrieve an AED within the stated walking-distance rule.

sourceReferences.section: 2.2 (A) Ask someone to get an AED

contentBlocks.title: Breathing branch
contentBlocks.body: Look for chest rise and fall for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is not normal breathing. If breathing is absent or abnormal, or you are unsure, begin CPR. If breathing is normal, do not compress; keep monitoring while waiting for EMS.

sourceReferences.section: RCA adult BLS algorithm for lay rescuers

contentBlocks.title: Remote-area exception
contentBlocks.body: If a lone rescuer in a remote area has no way to activate EMS, assess responsiveness and breathing, start compressions immediately when normal breathing is absent, and continue for at least two minutes before leaving to seek help. This is an edge case, not the main flow.

contentBlocks.title: Healthcare-provider path
contentBlocks.body: Only the HCP-labelled path includes a carotid pulse check together with breathing for no more than 10 seconds. If there is no definite pulse or there is doubt, the trained provider assumes arrest and starts compressions. The lay path does not ask learners to check a pulse.

contentBlocks.title: Guideline update: speaker mode and connected response
contentBlocks.body: Current sources emphasise speaker-phone dispatcher-assisted CPR and describe dispatcher support for AED location and nearby volunteer responders. The app rehearses that current flow while keeping every call simulated.

lessons.title: Hands-only CPR
lessons.summary: Adult positioning, hand placement, rhythm, recoil, interruptions and honest sensing limits.

learningObjectives.statement: Set up the casualty and adult hand position on the supported compression landmark.
Practise a 100–120-per-minute rhythm with full recoil and minimal interruption.
State the stop conditions and the app's depth-assessment limitation.

contentBlocks.title: Firm, flat surface
contentBlocks.body: Place the casualty on their back on a firm, flat surface before compressions. If the casualty must be rolled, support and turn the head, neck and body together.

contentBlocks.title: Landmark and xiphoid avoidance
contentBlocks.body: Locate the lower half of the sternum at the centre of the chest. Expose enough of the chest to place the hands accurately, keeping pressure away from the xiphoid process at the sternum's lower tip.

contentBlocks.title: Adult hand position and posture
contentBlocks.body: Kneel beside the casualty. Put one hand heel on the lower half of the sternum and the other on top, interlace and lift the fingers away from the chest wall, lock both elbows, bring the shoulders above the chest and use body weight.

contentBlocks.title: Rate and the 110 practice tempo
contentBlocks.body: The sourced adult compression rate is 100–120 per minute. The authored rhythm exercise uses 110 beats per minute as a practice tempo inside that approved band; 110 is not a separate guideline target. A live metronome remains dependent on the practice-view implementation.

contentBlocks.title: Full recoil
contentBlocks.body: Let the chest recoil completely after each compression while keeping the heels of the hands in contact with the chest.

contentBlocks.title: Count and control interruptions
contentBlocks.body: Count aloud in cycles of five up to 100 to support rhythm and tracking. Keep compressions continuous. If a lone rescuer becomes tired, any rest should be no longer than 10 seconds and preferably only after about 100 compressions, followed by an immediate restart.

contentBlocks.title: Depth — Not physically assessed
contentBlocks.body: The supplied sources teach an adult depth of 4–6 cm. Lifesaver Vision hand tracking cannot measure real depth or force, so the course labels depth and force ‘Not physically assessed’. No score may use a fabricated depth value; only supported placement, rhythm, interruption and posture signals are eligible.

contentBlocks.title: When to stop compressions
contentBlocks.body: Continue until paramedics or an in-facility emergency team take over, the AED says it is analysing, charging or about to shock, or the casualty wakes or resumes normal breathing. The lay path does not add a pulse check.

contentBlocks.title: Hands-only default
contentBlocks.body: A rescuer who is untrained, unable or unwilling to give ventilations should provide continuous high-quality chest compressions. A trained, able and willing rescuer may use 30 compressions to 2 breaths, with each breath over one second while watching for chest rise.

interactiveActivities.title: 110 BPM rhythm practice
interactiveActivities.instructions: Use a 110 BPM reference tempo to practise inside the approved 100–120 range. Review only supported rhythm, hand-placement, interruption and posture signals; depth and force remain Not physically assessed.

questions.prompt: What surface and position are needed for effective CPR?

choices.text: The casualty on their back on a firm, flat surface
The casualty seated upright on a soft sofa
The casualty standing against a wall
The casualty face down on a mattress

questions.explanation: Effective CPR requires the casualty to lie on their back on a firm, flat surface.

questions.prompt: Where should adult chest compressions be delivered?

choices.text: At the centre of the chest over the lower half of the sternum, avoiding the xiphoid process
Directly over the xiphoid process
Over the left collarbone
Over the abdomen below the ribs

questions.explanation: Use the lower half of the sternum at the centre of the chest and avoid the xiphoid process.

questions.prompt: Which description matches adult hand and body position for compressions?

choices.text: One hand heel on the lower sternum, the other on top, fingers interlaced and lifted, elbows straight, shoulders above the chest
Both palms flat on the abdomen with elbows bent
Fingertips on the collarbone with shoulders behind the hips
One hand over the xiphoid process and the other on the neck

questions.explanation: Correct positioning uses stacked hand heels on the lower sternum, interlaced lifted fingers, straight elbows and shoulders directly above the chest.

questions.prompt: What adult compression-depth range is stated in the source?

choices.text: At least 4 cm and not more than 6 cm
1 to 2 cm
Exactly 8 cm
More than 10 cm

questions.explanation: The source states an adult depth range of at least 4 cm and not more than 6 cm.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe supported compression rhythm and recoil? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Use a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute
Allow full recoil after every compression
Keep the hand heels in contact with the chest between compressions
Use fewer than 40 compressions per minute
Lean continuously so the chest cannot recoil

questions.explanation: Use 100 to 120 compressions per minute and allow complete recoil while keeping the hand heels in contact with the chest.

questions.prompt: Which rules correctly limit interruptions or define when CPR stops? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A tired lone rescuer may rest for no more than ten seconds, preferably after about 100 compressions
Pause when the AED prompts analysis, charging or shock
Stop when paramedics take over or the casualty wakes or resumes normal breathing
Take an unrestricted break after every ten compressions
Stop permanently as soon as the AED arrives, before it gives a prompt

questions.explanation: Keep interruptions brief. The supported stop conditions are emergency-team takeover, AED analysis/charging/shock prompts, or the casualty waking or regaining normal breathing.

contentBlocks.title: What the AED does
contentBlocks.body: An AED reads the heart rhythm through its pads, decides whether a shock is needed, charges only for a shockable rhythm and guides the rescuer with voice prompts. Some devices also provide a compression-tempo count.

contentBlocks.title: Bring an AED to every arrest

contentBlocks.title: Hair at a pad site

contentBlocks.title: Pacemaker or implanted defibrillator

contentBlocks.title: Medication patches and electrodes

contentBlocks.title: Wet or sweaty chest

contentBlocks.title: Adult AED application — steps 1–10
contentBlocks.body: 1. Keep compressions going as the AED arrives. 2. Open the case. 3. Switch on the AED. 4. Expose the chest. 5. Make the chest and surroundings ready for safe pad contact. 6. Open the pads and follow their pictures. 7. Place the right pad below the right collarbone. 8. Place the left pad below and left of the left nipple. 9. Plug in the connector if it is not pre-connected. 10. Stop contact only when the AED announces analysis, spread your arms and state ‘Stay Clear’.

contentBlocks.title: Eleven AED learning states
contentBlocks.body: The academy uses eleven project-authored states to rehearse the sourced flow: Awaiting AED; Power On; Prepare Chest; Apply Right Pad; Apply Left Pad; Connect Pads; Analyse — Clear; Charge — Clear; Clear Check and Shock; No Shock Advised; Resume CPR. These labels organise interaction and do not alter the AED's own prompts.

sourceReferences.section: C-5 summary of AED application sequence

contentBlocks.title: Adult pad placement
contentBlocks.body: Match the diagrams on the pads: position one high on the right chest beneath the collarbone and the other lower and farther out on the left chest, below the left nipple. Attach the lead if the AED model requires it.

contentBlocks.title: Analysis means nobody touches
contentBlocks.body: When the AED announces analysis, stop compressions. Nobody touches the casualty. Spread both arms and clearly state ‘Stay Clear’.

contentBlocks.title: Charge, clear-check and shock
contentBlocks.body: For a shockable rhythm the AED charges itself. Keep everyone clear. When the AED prompts for a shock, say ‘Stay Clear’, visually confirm that nobody is touching the casualty, then press the shock button firmly.

contentBlocks.title: Resume after a shock
contentBlocks.body: Restart chest compressions immediately after the shock and continue until the AED announces its next analysis. Current guidance states that re-analysis repeats every two minutes.

contentBlocks.title: Resume after no-shock advice
contentBlocks.body: If the AED advises no shock, restart continuous compressions immediately. Continue until the emergency team takes over, the AED directs that nobody touch the casualty, or the casualty resumes normal breathing.

contentBlocks.title: Keep the AED connected
contentBlocks.body: Leave the AED switched on and connected throughout, including after normal breathing returns and during transport.

contentBlocks.title: Guideline update: two-minute re-analysis
contentBlocks.body: The 2018 flow showed repeat analysis without naming the interval. Current supplied guidance makes the two-minute re-analysis cycle explicit.

contentBlocks.title: Never shock while anyone is touching
contentBlocks.body: Nobody may touch the casualty during analysis, charging or shock. Before choosing the simulated shock action, state the clear command, spread both arms and visually confirm that nobody is touching. The project classifies contact here as a critical error, and the interaction implementation must fail closed unless the clear check is satisfied.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 1 — unsafe location
contentBlocks.body: Identify traffic, fire, a wet floor or falling objects. Move the casualty only when the found location is unsafe or unsuitable, then use a safe, flat, open space.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 2 — remote area without phone access
contentBlocks.body: Use the documented remote exception: assess responsiveness and breathing, start compressions when normal breathing is absent, continue for at least two minutes, then leave to seek help.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 3 — metal surface
contentBlocks.body: Move the casualty away from metal contact before AED use because the surface can conduct current towards the rescuer.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 4 — wet chest or surface
contentBlocks.body: Move away from the wet surface and wipe the chest dry quickly so the pads can adhere.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 5 — flammable gas or oxygen source
contentBlocks.body: Before AED use, create safe distance between the casualty and any flammable gas or oxygen source.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 6 — hair prevents contact
contentBlocks.body: Shave only the pad sites promptly when chest hair prevents secure adhesion.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 7 — jewellery, patches and implanted device
contentBlocks.body: Move metallic chains away, remove medication patches or monitoring electrodes, and keep the pads at least four fingers' breadth from a visible implanted device.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 8 — break-glass AED cabinet
contentBlocks.body: Use a phone, shoe, keys or another object rather than bare hands or elbows, and clear glass from the edge before reaching for the key.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 9 — trolley bed and team
contentBlocks.body: Use a step stool on a trolley bed so elbows can remain straight. With two or more rescuers, divide compressions, 995 activation and AED tasks; allocate ventilations only within the trained, able and willing pathway.

contentBlocks.title: Drill 10 — narrow space or aircraft
contentBlocks.body: In a narrow space, the sourced alternative is compressing from above the casualty's head. On an aircraft, kneel in the seat leg space unless the casualty can be moved quickly to the galley.

criticalActions.title: Assess and secure the scene
criticalActions.actionDescription: Check for danger first. Continue only in a safe setting; if the site is unsafe or unsuitable, move the casualty to a safe, flat, open space as soon as possible.

criticalActions.title: Check responsiveness
criticalActions.actionDescription: Make firm contact at both shoulders and call out a simple question to check for any response. Do not jolt the casualty, and keep neck movement to a minimum.

feedbackStatements.statement: The responsiveness check uses a firm shoulder tap and a loud verbal prompt.

criticalActions.title: Activate emergency help
criticalActions.actionDescription: Use the clearly marked SIMULATION 995 flow. If alone, rehearse speaker mode, stay on the line, and follow the dispatcher; an in-facility emergency response system may be activated where applicable.

feedbackStatements.statement: The simulated call keeps the learner with the casualty and follows dispatcher guidance.

criticalActions.title: Manage AED retrieval
criticalActions.actionDescription: Ask another person to fetch an AED when it is within about a 60-second walk. A lone rescuer stays with the casualty and does not leave to search.

criticalActions.title: Check normal breathing
criticalActions.actionDescription: Look for chest rise and fall for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is not normal breathing; absent, abnormal or uncertain breathing leads to CPR, while normal breathing leads to continued monitoring.

feedbackStatements.statement: The breathing decision separates the monitoring path from the immediate-CPR path.

criticalActions.title: Position for CPR
criticalActions.actionDescription: For the CPR branch, place the casualty on their back on a firm, flat surface, supporting the head, neck and body together if a turn is needed.

feedbackStatements.statement: A firm, flat, supine position supports effective compressions.

criticalActions.title: Perform hands-only compressions
criticalActions.actionDescription: For absent, abnormal or uncertain breathing, compress over the lower half of the sternum and avoid the xiphoid process; maintain 100–120 compressions per minute, full recoil and minimal interruptions.

feedbackStatements.statement: Keep placement, rhythm, recoil and interruptions within the source-backed adult practice rules.

criticalActions.title: Prepare and apply the AED
criticalActions.actionDescription: Keep compressions going wherever possible while powering on, resolving hazards, preparing the chest, applying the right then left adult pads, and connecting the pads when required.

criticalActions.title: Clear for analysis and shock

criticalActions.title: Resume CPR after the AED decision

criticalErrors.remediation: Repeat the SIMULATION activation step, using speaker mode when alone and following dispatcher guidance.

feedbackStatements.statement: The emergency response must be activated as part of DRSABC.

criticalErrors.title: Lone rescuer leaves for an AED
criticalErrors.errorDescription: On the alone branch, the learner leaves the casualty to search for an AED.
criticalErrors.remediation: Stay with the casualty; use speaker mode for the simulated 995 call and ask another person to fetch the AED when one becomes available.

feedbackStatements.statement: A lone rescuer must remain with the casualty rather than leaving to search for an AED.

criticalErrors.title: Gasping treated as normal breathing
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner interprets gasping as normal breathing and withholds chest compressions.
criticalErrors.remediation: Repeat the breathing branch: gasping is abnormal and requires immediate CPR.

feedbackStatements.statement: Gasping is not the normal-breathing branch.

criticalErrors.title: Compressions started during normal breathing
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner starts chest compressions after identifying that the casualty is breathing normally.
criticalErrors.remediation: Use the monitoring branch when breathing is normal and wait for EMS.

feedbackStatements.statement: Do not start compressions when normal breathing is present.

sourceReferences.section: RCA adult BLS algorithm for lay rescuers

criticalErrors.title: Compression over the xiphoid area
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner places the compression target over the xiphoid process rather than the lower half of the sternum.
criticalErrors.remediation: Reset hand placement to the centre of the chest over the lower half of the sternum and avoid the xiphoid process.

feedbackStatements.statement: Correct the hand-placement zone before resuming the practice sequence.

criticalErrors.title: Adult pads placed incorrectly
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner does not follow the adult pad pictures or places either pad outside the supported right-chest and left-chest positions.
criticalErrors.remediation: Reapply the right pad below the right collarbone and the left pad below and left of the left nipple, following the pad pictures.

feedbackStatements.statement: Reset the adult pads to the source-backed positions before analysis.

criticalErrors.title: Contact during AED analysis
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner or another person remains in contact with the casualty while the AED is analysing.
criticalErrors.remediation: Repeat the analysis clear sequence: stop compressions, spread the arms, say “Stay Clear”, and confirm nobody is touching.

feedbackStatements.statement: AED analysis requires a complete no-touch clear check.

criticalErrors.title: Shock attempted without a clear check
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner presses the shock control without first keeping everybody clear, repeating the clear call and visually confirming no contact.
criticalErrors.remediation: Repeat charging and shock delivery with nobody touching and a visible clear check before pressing the control.

feedbackStatements.statement: Never deliver the prompted shock while anybody is touching the casualty.

criticalErrors.title: CPR not resumed after AED outcome
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner delays or omits restarting chest compressions after a delivered shock or a no-shock announcement.
criticalErrors.remediation: Restart compressions immediately after either AED outcome.

feedbackStatements.statement: Both shock and no-shock paths require an immediate return to compressions.

criticalErrors.title: CPR stopped without a supported condition
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner stops CPR when there is no emergency-team takeover, AED analysis/charging/shock prompt, waking, or return of normal breathing.

feedbackStatements.statement: Do not end compressions for an unsupported reason.

If breathing is normal, monitor and wait for EMS rather than starting compressions.

criticalActions.title: Assess and secure the scene

criticalActions.title: Assess and secure the scene
criticalActions.actionDescription: Check for danger first. Continue only in a safe setting; if the site is unsafe or unsuitable, move the casualty to a safe, flat, open space as soon as possible.

feedbackStatements.statement: Good scene assessment protects both rescuer and casualty before the response continues.

criticalActions.title: Check responsiveness
criticalActions.actionDescription: Make firm contact at both shoulders and call out a simple question to check for any response. Do not jolt the casualty, and keep neck movement to a minimum.

feedbackStatements.statement: The responsiveness check uses a firm shoulder tap and a loud verbal prompt.

criticalActions.title: Activate emergency help
criticalActions.actionDescription: Use the clearly marked SIMULATION 995 flow. If alone, rehearse speaker mode, stay on the line, and follow the dispatcher; an in-facility emergency response system may be activated where applicable.

feedbackStatements.statement: The simulated call keeps the learner with the casualty and follows dispatcher guidance.

criticalActions.title: Manage AED retrieval
criticalActions.actionDescription: Ask another person to fetch an AED when it is within about a 60-second walk. A lone rescuer stays with the casualty and does not leave to search.

criticalActions.title: Check normal breathing
criticalActions.actionDescription: Look for chest rise and fall for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is not normal breathing; absent, abnormal or uncertain breathing leads to CPR, while normal breathing leads to continued monitoring.

feedbackStatements.statement: The breathing decision separates the monitoring path from the immediate-CPR path.

criticalActions.title: Position for CPR
criticalActions.actionDescription: For the CPR branch, place the casualty on their back on a firm, flat surface, supporting the head, neck and body together if a turn is needed.

feedbackStatements.statement: A firm, flat, supine position supports effective compressions.

criticalActions.title: Perform hands-only compressions
criticalActions.actionDescription: For absent, abnormal or uncertain breathing, compress over the lower half of the sternum and avoid the xiphoid process; maintain 100–120 compressions per minute, full recoil and minimal interruptions.

feedbackStatements.statement: Keep placement, rhythm, recoil and interruptions within the source-backed adult practice rules.

criticalActions.title: Prepare and apply the AED
criticalActions.actionDescription: Keep compressions going wherever possible while powering on, resolving hazards, preparing the chest, applying the right then left adult pads, and connecting the pads when required.

feedbackStatements.statement: The AED sequence preserves compressions while preparation and pad placement are completed.

criticalActions.title: Clear for analysis and shock
criticalActions.actionDescription: Stop compressions when analysis is announced and ensure nobody touches the casualty. If a shock is advised, keep clear during charging, repeat the clear call, visually check contact, then press the shock control when prompted.

feedbackStatements.statement: Nobody touches the casualty during AED analysis, charging or shock delivery.

criticalActions.title: Resume CPR after the AED decision
criticalActions.actionDescription: Restart chest compressions immediately after a delivered shock or a no-shock announcement and continue until the next AED analysis or another supported stop condition.

feedbackStatements.statement: Both AED outcomes return directly to chest compressions.

criticalActions.title: Communicate clearly
criticalActions.actionDescription: Give the simulated dispatcher the requested incident details, follow the coaching, and use an audible clear call before analysis and any shock.

feedbackStatements.statement: Clear spoken communication supports dispatcher guidance and the AED no-touch checks.

criticalActions.title: Minimise avoidable delay
criticalActions.actionDescription: Move through recognition, compressions and AED use without avoidable delay while preserving every scene-safety and no-touch check.

feedbackStatements.statement: Prompt action matters, but speed never removes a required safety or clear check.

criticalActions.title: Monitor normal breathing
criticalActions.actionDescription: On the normal-breathing branch, do not start compressions; continue monitoring and wait for EMS.

feedbackStatements.statement: Normal breathing leads to monitoring rather than chest compressions.

criticalErrors.title: Responsiveness not checked

criticalErrors.title: Emergency help not activated

criticalErrors.remediation: Stay with the casualty; use speaker mode for the simulated 995 call and ask another person to fetch the AED when one becomes available.

feedbackStatements.statement: A lone rescuer must remain with the casualty rather than leaving to search for an AED.

criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner interprets gasping as normal breathing and withholds chest compressions.

feedbackStatements.statement: Gasping is not the normal-breathing branch.

criticalErrors.title: Compressions started during normal breathing
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner starts chest compressions after identifying that the casualty is breathing normally.

criticalErrors.title: Compression over the xiphoid area
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner places the compression target over the xiphoid process rather than the lower half of the sternum.
criticalErrors.remediation: Reset hand placement to the centre of the chest over the lower half of the sternum and avoid the xiphoid process.

feedbackStatements.statement: Correct the hand-placement zone before resuming the practice sequence.

criticalErrors.title: Adult pads placed incorrectly
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner does not follow the adult pad pictures or places either pad outside the supported right-chest and left-chest positions.

criticalErrors.title: Contact during AED analysis
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner or another person remains in contact with the casualty while the AED is analysing.
criticalErrors.remediation: Repeat the analysis clear sequence: stop compressions, spread the arms, say “Stay Clear”, and confirm nobody is touching.

feedbackStatements.statement: AED analysis requires a complete no-touch clear check.

criticalErrors.title: Shock attempted without a clear check
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner presses the shock control without first keeping everybody clear, repeating the clear call and visually confirming no contact.
criticalErrors.remediation: Repeat charging and shock delivery with nobody touching and a visible clear check before pressing the control.

feedbackStatements.statement: Never deliver the prompted shock while anybody is touching the casualty.

criticalErrors.title: CPR not resumed after AED outcome
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner delays or omits restarting chest compressions after a delivered shock or a no-shock announcement.
criticalErrors.remediation: Restart compressions immediately after either AED outcome.

feedbackStatements.statement: Both shock and no-shock paths require an immediate return to compressions.

criticalErrors.title: CPR stopped without a supported condition
criticalErrors.errorDescription: The learner stops CPR when there is no emergency-team takeover, AED analysis/charging/shock prompt, waking, or return of normal breathing.
criticalErrors.remediation: Continue CPR until one of the source-backed stop conditions occurs.

contentBlocks.title: LOCKED — awareness only
contentBlocks.body: This module requires completion of Modules 0–8, qualified instructor approval and a clinically approved course lifecycle. It is not paediatric certification, contains no scored assessment and must not be used to infer technique beyond the cited extract.

contentBlocks.title: Why paediatric arrest may differ
contentBlocks.body: The 2022 manual states that paediatric out-of-hospital arrest is usually non-cardiac and most cases begin with a non-shockable rhythm, so ventilation and oxygenation are important. It also reports shockable initial rhythms in about 5–19% of cases, particularly among school-age children and adolescents.

contentBlocks.title: Early AED awareness
contentBlocks.body: The supplied 2022 manual states that ILCOR supports early AED use for a child in cardiac arrest. It reports higher survival among children with shockable rhythms treated early than among children presenting with other rhythms.

sourceReferences.section: 3.9 Recommendation for AED Use in Children

contentBlocks.title: Child pad system — SME decision required
contentBlocks.body: The 2022 manual uses an age-based 1–12-year paediatric dose-attenuation rule, while the 2021 summary uses a body-weight threshold below 25 kg. A qualified SME must set one canonical learner-facing rule before this content can be approved.

sourceReferences.section: 3.9 Recommendation for AED Use in Children

contentBlocks.title: Infant defibrillation — SME decision required
contentBlocks.body: For an infant, the 2021 summary places a manual defibrillator first and child pads next when the preferred device is unavailable. None of the supplied sources gives a clear adult-pad instruction for an infant, so the course withholds one pending SME approval.

sourceReferences.section: CPR summary table, use of AED (infant column)

contentBlocks.title: Adult pads on a child
contentBlocks.body: For a child, the 2022 manual permits an AED with adult pads when no paediatric system is available. Pads must not touch or overlap; with adult pads, use front-and-back placement with one pad on the central sternum and one on the upper back between the shoulder blades.

contentBlocks.title: Paediatric pad separation
contentBlocks.body: For front-of-chest paediatric pad placement, follow the pad pictures and keep the pads from touching or overlapping, with at least 2 cm between them.

sourceReferences.section: 3.9 Placement of Defibrillation Pads for Children/Infant

contentBlocks.title: Compression values and methods — SME review
contentBlocks.body: The supplied 2021 summary contains child and infant depth, landmark, method and full-recoil details, but neither provider manual teaches the paediatric technique. Lifesaver Vision keeps these items at awareness level and does not release technique coaching until SME approval.

contentBlocks.title: Infant response and HCP ratios — SME review

contentBlocks.title: Handover essentials
contentBlocks.body: Share the estimated collapse time, whether the AED was applied and the recorded shock count. Add any known medical history, medicines and written event notes.

contentBlocks.title: Assist and leave the AED connected
contentBlocks.body: Continue assisting until the casualty is loaded into the ambulance. Keep the AED switched on, with pads and cable attached, during transport.

contentBlocks.title: After normal breathing returns
contentBlocks.body: Keep the casualty lying on their back and monitor continuously until help arrives. Leave the AED pads connected.

contentBlocks.title: Guideline update: no recovery position in this flow
contentBlocks.body: Current guidance no longer recommends the recovery position after cardiac arrest because it may conceal a re-arrest. Keep the casualty supine, monitor continuously and leave the AED attached. Recovery-position technique is outside this course flow.

contentBlocks.title: AED owner follow-up
contentBlocks.body: Notify the facility or safety manager. The owner or vendor replaces used consumables, checks the battery, repairs the cabinet where needed and can retrieve the AED event record for audit.

contentBlocks.title: Operational update: battery cadence needs local confirmation
